fields.label: The meeting
fields.text: In 45 minutes, you ask your questions about the project and see where your money goes and when it can come back.

fields.label: The sample project
fields.name: Tavessa, in Fort Pierce, Florida
fields.text: Tavessa is a residential rental building in Fort Pierce, Florida. With EB-5, you invest in the company behind a project like this one, which creates the jobs the law requires, and you don't receive an apartment.
fields.caption: Aerial view of Tavessa, a fictional project created for this page.
fields.imageAlt: Aerial view of the white residential building on the lagoon, with a dock and two boats, a boat passing on the water, palm trees around it, a marina and a bridge in the background

fields.label: Topics
fields.heading: What you can cover in the meeting
fields.intro: Six topics, with time for your questions.

items.heading: How EB-5 works
items.text: Each step between the investment and the green card, in order, and what the law requires of the business that receives the money.
items.imageAlt: A building under construction with two cranes and its concrete frame exposed

items.heading: How much to invest
items.text: The minimum is $1,050,000 and drops to $800,000 in a targeted employment area (TEA), which means a rural area or one with high unemployment. You see what the inflation adjustment changes for petitions filed in 2027 or later.
items.imageAlt: A white scale model of an apartment building with a pool on a wooden table, with a ruler, a pencil and a rolled drawing beside it

items.heading: Regional center or direct investment
items.text: A regional center is an entity approved by USCIS, the U.S. immigration agency, that pools several investors in the same project. You see how each path reaches the 10 jobs required per investor, all of them full time.
items.imageAlt: A printed site plan on a wooden table, with a pen and a cup of coffee

items.heading: Source of funds
items.text: How to document where the invested money came from. The examples cover the sale of a home or a company in Brazil, an inheritance and a loan.
items.imageAlt: A stack of light folders tied with a ribbon, with a fountain pen on top

items.heading: Risk and getting your capital back
items.text: Where your money sits in the project, what happens if construction runs late and what repayment of your capital depends on. {brand} doesn't promise a return, and the meeting shows you why.
items.imageAlt: Concrete columns and slabs of a building under construction, with rebar showing

items.heading: Family, timing and taxes
items.text: Which family members are included, what the timing depends on and what the green card changes in the tax on your income from Brazil. You leave with the questions to take to your tax advisor.
items.imageAlt: A kitchen with a marble island, wood cabinets and a window facing palm trees

items.heading: Live in the U.S. with your family
items.text: See the whole path before you hire an attorney.
items.imageAlt: A couple and their two sons, seen from behind on an apartment balcony, watching the sunset over the water

items.heading: Invest in U.S. real estate
items.text: Learn what EB-5 requires beyond the money.
items.imageAlt: A man with gray hair in a light linen jacket, leaning over floor plans on a wooden table, next to the white scale model of an apartment building with a pool, with the lagoon behind him

items.heading: Stay in the U.S. for good
items.text: For people who live there on a temporary visa and want the green card.
items.imageAlt: A woman in a light blazer with a bag on her shoulder walking on a stone sidewalk between palm trees and houses

fields.heading: EB-5 visa risks: what can go wrong
fields.intro: The questions people ask about EB-5, answered with no promises.

timeline.legend: Solid line: what the law sets. Dashed line: what depends on the project.

items.title: Investment
items.text: The capital goes into the project.

items.title: 2 years
items.text: The minimum time the law requires the capital to stay invested.

items.title: Repayment
items.text: Depends on how the project performs. It isn't guaranteed.

items.question: Do I need to bring any documents?

answer.text: No. The meeting is for your questions. Documents on the source of funds and on immigration stay with your attorney.

items.question: Does buying a home in the U.S. get me a green card?

answer.text: No. With EB-5, the money goes into a business that creates at least 10 jobs, all of them full time. USCIS says that owning a home to live in doesn't count as that business. In Tavessa, the sample project, you invest in the project company and you don't receive an apartment.

items.question: Can I lose the money I invest?

answer.text: Yes. EB-5 requires the capital to stay invested for at least 2 years in a business, and that business can lose money. In the meeting, Rafael Moura shows where the money goes in the project and which risks stay with the investor.

items.question: When and how does my capital come back?

answer.text: The law requires the capital to stay invested for at least 2 years. After that, repayment depends on how the project performs, and it isn't guaranteed. The SEC, the U.S. securities regulator, and USCIS say to be suspicious of anyone who promises to give your money back. The offering documents state the conditions for repayment, and Rafael Moura shows in the meeting where to read them.

items.question: Does my green card depend on the project?

answer.text: In part, yes. The first green card is conditional, for 2 years. You file Form I-829 to remove the conditions in the 90 days before it expires. With Form I-829, you show that you kept the capital invested for the 2 years and that the project created the 10 jobs, or will create them within a reasonable time. That's why the project's progress matters for that filing. If USCIS denies Form I-829, the investor, the spouse and the children lose the green card as of the date of the decision. You can ask for a review only in the removal proceedings that USCIS opens next. Your immigration attorney tells you what a delay changes in your case.

Your spouse and your unmarried children under 21 are included. They receive the same conditional green card, for 2 years, as the investor. The law doesn't include the investor's parents in the petition. If a child is close to turning 21, take the case to your attorney.

items.question: What is the EB-5 processing time?

answer.text: No one can guarantee the timing, {brand} included. Review time depends on USCIS, and the green card depends on a visa being available. In the meeting, our team lays out the steps in order (the petition, the conditional green card for 2 years and Form I-829).

items.question: Can I live in the U.S. while I wait?

answer.text: It depends on where you are. If you're in Brazil, you apply to the U.S. government for the immigrant visa, from outside the U.S., after the petition is approved. If you're already in the U.S., you can apply for the green card together with the petition when a visa is available. Your immigration attorney tells you which path applies to you.

items.question: How do I prove the source of my funds?

answer.text: With documents that show where the money came from and that it was obtained lawfully, such as the sale of a home or a company. The law asks the same for the money used for fees and lists, as applicable, business records and tax returns from the past 7 years. Borrowed or gifted money counts only if it was lent or given in good faith, and the law asks for records from the donor and from the lender, unless the lender is a bank. Your attorney puts your set of documents together.

items.question: Will I pay U.S. tax on what I have in Brazil?

answer.text: The IRS, the U.S. tax agency, treats green card holders as U.S. tax residents. A resident reports worldwide income on the U.S. tax return, and that includes income from Brazil. How much you pay depends on your case. Take the question to a tax advisor who knows both countries before you invest.

items.question: What if the rules change midway?

answer.text: Today, the Regional Center Program, which pools several investors in the same project, is authorized through September 30, 2027. The law tells the government to keep processing petitions filed on or before September 30, 2026, even if that authorization ends. That date has passed. Ask your attorney what applies to a petition filed now.
{brand} doesn't promise a return. Each project's terms are in the offering documents, and {brand} shares those documents only with accredited investors.

items.question: What should I ask before I invest?

answer.text: Be wary of anyone who guarantees a green card, a timeline or a return. {brand} guarantees none of them. Before you send any money, ask for the offering documents in writing and take these questions to your attorney:

list: Did the earlier projects repay the investors' capital?
How much of its own money did the developer put into the project?
Does the contract allow my money to be moved to another project without my choice?
Is the loan to the project backed by collateral?
Is the person who referred me paid a commission?

answer.text: After the meeting, the next step is a conversation with an immigration attorney of your choice.
